newsitem.title: GERMANY: TIETMEYER SAYS HOPEFUL FOR AGREEMENT IN DUBLIN.
newsitem.headline: TIETMEYER SAYS HOPEFUL FOR AGREEMENT IN DUBLIN.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Tuesday that Germany and France must still make major steps for a solid European currency union.

Tietmeyer also said criteria for currency union laid out in the Maastricht Treaty must be properly and precisely applied and that countries joining the new currency must be able to show they can maintain lasting stability.
"The goal is to ensure lasting growth and employment," he told a news conference after a Franco-German economic summit. But he stressed, "The criteria must be properly applied."
Tietmeyer said he was hopeful for progress toward a stability pact to be implemented after currency union at upcoming European Union meetings in Dublin.
"We have agreed that a stability pact is necessary and that it must be an efficient one," Tietmeyer told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
"I am very hopeful that we can come to a result," he said.
European finance and economics ministers are scheduled to meet this weekend in Dublin for an informal session and then return to Dublin in December for a formal meeting.
No official decisions are reached at the informal meetings but the groundwork for the later meeting are made.
Tietmeyer also said he was very hopeful for an agreement at the Dublin meetings on "ins" and "pre-ins".
When asked whether a decision will be taken on the relationship between countries who will participate in the launch of the single currency and those outside, he said:
"I hope so, because on the agenda of the Dublin meeting will be on one hand the stability pact and also the so-called pre-ins and outs relationship."
Tietmeyer also said that the German yield curve, which he believed was too steep, can only flatten if financial markets are confident of the success of currency union.

"Capital market rates must come down further. The yield curve is currently too steep. But that can only happen if markets have trust" in efforts by European nations to meet Maastricht Treaty criteria, Tietmeyer said.
